front: Why is one-hot a poor word representation?
back: Sparse (size of vocabulary), and all distinct words are orthogonal at distance $\sqrt2$: no similarity structure.
A word's meaning is given by the contexts it appears in ("you shall know a word by the company it keeps", Firth).
Skip-gram predicts context words from the centre word (better for rare words); CBOW predicts the centre from the summed context (good for frequent words).
$V$ holds centre-word vectors (first layer), $U$ context-word vectors (output layer). Keep $V$ or $V+U$ as the embedding.
The full softmax costs $O(nd)$ per pair; negative sampling updates only $1+k$ context rows and one centre row: $O((k+1)d)$.

front: Loss when all vectors are zero

back: $a^\top b/(\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert)\in[-1,1]$. Scale-invariant; preferred to Euclidean distance for embeddings.

front: How to answer an analogy a:b::c:?

back: $\sum f(X_{ij})(w_i^\top\tilde w_j+b_i+\tilde b_j-\log X_{ij})^2$ with $f$ damping very frequent pairs; embedding $=w+\tilde w$.

front: Why does GloVe use the log of co-occurrence probabilities?
back: Ratios $P(k|i)/P(k|j)$ separate meaningful axes; the log turns them into differences $(w_i-w_j)^\top\tilde w_k$, so analogies become vector offsets.
Word vector = sum of embeddings of its character n-grams (plus the word). Unseen words still get a vector; handles morphology.

front: Main limits of static word embeddings
back: One vector per word type (no polysemy), no word order, corpus biases, and antonyms can end up close because contexts are similar.
